<1>6.3.2 </1>On functional value equivalence as a parameter of the lawfulness of alterations

Functional value equivalence operates as a criterion of the lawfulness of unilateral alterations made in continuous digital services that administer Immaterial Objects of Consumption. The starting point lies in the feature whereby, in IOCs, the legal problem is not solved merely by asking whether the object still “exists”, whether the account remains accessible or whether some formal trace of the acquisition is still standing. What must be controlled is whether the mutation made by the supplier substantially preserves the core of enjoyment that made the acquisition rational and legitimizes the consumer's remaining in the relationship. In continuing relationships, protection is not satisfied by the nominal survival of the performance, because the minimum basis of the contract also includes the legitimate expectations of utility and continuity built over the course of execution<1><2>734</2></1>. It is precisely for this reason that functional value equivalence presents itself as a more adequate parameter than a reading centered only on abstract ownership or on the formal permanence of the asset: what the system must protect is the integrity of enjoyment, and not the mere appearance that “something is still there”.

This formulation does not require rigid equality between before and after. Functional value equivalence does not mean freezing the object, literal repetition of attributes, absolute <1>p. 649</1> maintenance of <2>layout</2>, <3>stats</3><4><5>735</5></4>, parameters or isolated micro-characteristics. The <6>standard</6> does not prohibit the evolution of the service, the adaptation of the ecosystem, the balancing of mechanics or the ordinary innovation inherent to continuous platforms and games. What it requires is substantial preservation of the performance, the practical utility and the role played by the object in the governed environment, considering the objectifiable reasons that justified the consumer's acquisition and remaining<7><8>736</8></7>. In other words, the legally relevant question is not whether everything remained identical, but whether the object continues to serve, at a functionally equivalent level, the ends that legitimately justified the contracting and the maintenance of the relationship <9>Miragem</9><10>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 521; p. 523])</10>.

This equivalence, however, is not exhausted by narrow technical functionality. In IOCs, functional value may comprise ecosystemic and, in certain cases, symbolic dimensions, provided they are objectifiable within the regime of enjoyment itself. This includes, for example, the capacity of use, performance, access and compatibility, but it may also reach the role of the object within the ecosystem, its relational relevance, its position of use, its density of rarity, its function of distinction or the way it integrates trajectory, status and recognition stabilized in the environment<1><2>737</2></1>. The point is not to turn every subjective preference into a legal claim, nor to open the door to touchiness disguised as dogmatics. The point is to recognize that, in governed ecosystems, certain symbolic and positional dimensions are not external <3>p. 650</3> adornments, but part of the very utility for which the consumer joins, remains and invests in the object. When these elements verifiably integrate the promised core of enjoyment, their degradation may be legally relevant even if the object remains formally accessible <4>Bessa</4><5>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 328; p. 246])</5>.

The dogmatic premise of this construction lies in the treatment of continuing and dependent relationships. The parallel with long-term captive contracts does not enter here as an automatic transplant or as academic ornament, but as disciplined interpretive infrastructure. In relationships of this nature, what is protected is not only the initial delivery, but the minimum stability of the performance program and the trust legitimately built over time<1><2>738</2></1>. The consumer does not adhere merely to an isolated utility, captured in a contractual snapshot of the first day. He binds himself to a relationship whose value depends on the minimally loyal preservation of the functional program of the performance. For this reason, readaptations and mutations are legally admissible, yes, but only insofar as they are compatible with the maintenance of the expected utility and with the non-frustration of the legitimate expectations that sustained joining and remaining in the relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</4>. The platform may change. What it may not do is convert mutability into a vehicle for the opportunistic downgrading of enjoyment under the pretext of mere evolution of the service.

It is at this point that the theory of objective good faith in lasting relationships gains a practical function. The lawfulness of the mutation is not measured by its mere abstract provision in a contractual clause, nor by the formal permanence of the object after the alteration. In prolonged relationships, change remains legitimate only when compatible with the functional continuity of the performance, with loyalty in execution and with the trust built by the supplier's prior conduct<1><2>739</2></1>. Unfavorable and harmful surprise, the abrupt rupture of patterns <3>p. 651</3> previously tolerated and the abrupt reconfiguration of the expected utility may characterize a breach of trust and a violation of the contractual program concretely lived, even if the contract remains nominally in force <4>Martins-Costa</4><5>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 45; p. 401)</5>. In less pompous and more useful language: it is not enough to leave the shell of the relationship intact if the content enjoyed has been emptied.

This requires recognizing that contractual balance, in long-term relationships, is not only the balance of the initial moment of agreement. There is also a dynamic synallagma, that is, a functional balance that accompanies the relationship over time<1><2>740</2></1>. In IOCs, this observation is pure gold, because the object is not consumed only at the moment of purchase; it is consumed along the iter of enjoyment, amid continuous updates, reconfigurations and mediations. Hence, the lawfulness of the alteration must be assessed in light of the functional unity of the relationship, and not only of the abstract existence of a generic authorization to change. If the modification relevantly breaks this functional unity, downgrades the expected utility and disorganizes the trust built, the formal permanence of the relationship no longer suffices as a criterion of legitimacy <3>Martins-Costa</3><4>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 75; p. 232)</4>.

Functional value equivalence, then, acts as a material test of legitimate mutability. Its field of application opens whenever there is an alteration with the potential to relevantly affect the practical function, the ecosystemic position, the symbolic density or the continuity of enjoyment of the IOC. The trigger is not any petty change, any visual touch-up or any marginal oscillation proper to the normal life of the service. The <1>standard</1> lights up when the platform brings about a downgrade of use, limitation of access, loss of compatibility, alteration of essential parameters, removal of functionalities, structural rebalancing, discontinuation of an ecosystemic role, degradation of relational position or emptying of attributes with objective weight in the rationale of the acquisition<2><3>741</3></2>. Unilateral <4>p. 652</4> alteration is already, in itself, legally sensitive under the CDC; and this sensitivity is aggravated when the change is not neutral, but results in a material reduction or impairment of the consumer's interest in the performance <5>Miragem</5><6>(Miragem, 2020, p. 387; p. 425)</6>.

To make this <1>standard</1> operable, it is advisable to structure it as an application test. The first step consists of identifying the functional core of the object. What practical utility justified the acquisition? What role did the object play in the ecosystem? Where pertinent, what symbolic, reputational or relational density was objectively incorporated into the enjoyment? Here, the analysis must not be psychologizing or folkloric. It does not matter whether the consumer “loved” that item. What matters is whether there was a verifiable core of utility, role and signification that integrated the legitimately formed expectation<2><3>742</3></2>. The offer and the trust it awakens provide a direct basis for this identification, since the consumer contracts in view of the advertised advantages and qualities, giving rise to the legal duty to maintain the offered conditions or, at least, to substantially preserve their utility <4>Miragem</4><5>(Miragem, 2020, p. 424)</5>.

The second step is to reconstruct the alteration and the impact. What exactly was modified? What is the before and after in terms of use, performance, access, compatibility, ecosystemic function, recognition, rarity, trajectory or continuity of experience? This examination cannot remain trapped in the formalism of “it still exists” or “it is still available”. Consumer-law inadequacy also sets in when the performance remains formally present, but no longer corresponds, in legal terms, to the legitimately expected quality, functionality or conformity. The CDC works with the functional defect precisely to reach nonconformities that frustrate the consumer's legitimate expectation without requiring the total disappearance of the object <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 246; p. 328])</2>.

<1>p. 653</1> The third step is to measure the relevance of the loss. Was there a marginal loss, inserted in the ordinary evolution of the service, or was there a substantial emptying of the functional core of enjoyment? Not every reduction is unlawful. Platforms are not wax museums. But there is a point beyond which the alteration ceases to be ordinary adaptation and begins to operate as a material downgrading of the use value acquired. It is here that the idea of the minimum basis of the relationship becomes central. If the fundamental legitimate expectations that sustained the contracting are excluded, the imbalance is no longer a detail: it becomes structural <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 292)</3>. Functional equivalence serves precisely to separate tolerable wear from legally intolerable corrosion.

The fourth step is to examine justification and restoration. Even when there is a relevant loss, the mutation may still be legally tolerable if there is verifiable justification and adequate restoration. Did the platform demonstrate, in a minimally auditable way, the technical or systemic reason for the change? Did it offer real alternatives, reversibility, a parallel version, equivalent functional substitution, correction of parameters, preservation of compatibility, restoration of status or another mechanism capable of substantially preserving enjoyment? This point matters a great deal because the CDC is not content with the mere finding of the problem. It structures remedies of material restoration, specific relief and a practical result equivalent to performance, both in the case of a quality defect and in the case of nonconformity with the offer <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 338; p. 408; p. 597])</2>. Thus, it is not enough merely to acknowledge the change and assert one's own power to carry it out. If the change was substantially relevant, restoration must necessarily be part of the discussion.

This test depends directly on the preceding <1>standard</1> of open auditability. There is no way to assess substantial preservation of functional value without a verifiable minimum about what was altered, when, why and with what effects. If the platform prevents reconstruction of the impact, opacity is not neutral. It becomes a dogmatic aggravating factor, because it makes impossible the control of adequacy, of trust and of the very legitimacy of the mutation. Functional equivalence without auditability becomes an elegant guess. With auditability, it becomes an institutionally manageable criterion.

The legal consequences of this construction are relevant. When there is no substantial preservation of functional value, the alteration tends to constitute a relevant inadequacy of supply. Depending on the structure of the case, this may be treated as a quality defect in the product or service, or, in more extreme situations of harm or risk, approach the logic of the safety defect. The main point, however, is that the nominal permanence of the object does not exclude the application of the protective regime. If the legitimately expected utility has been emptied, the inadequacy is already <1>p. 654</1> given, even if the account remains active and the item continues to be listed in the inventory <2>Miragem</2><3>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 521; p. 523])</3>.

In these cases, the priority protection must be functional restoration. The consumer-law system was not designed to automatically convert every relevant frustration into residual monetary compensation. In an IOC environment, the most legally adequate remedy is often to restore equivalence of enjoyment: reversal of the alteration, an alternative version, equivalent functional substitution, restoration of attributes, correction of parameters, preservation of trajectory, maintenance of compatibility or other measures capable of reestablishing, as far as possible, the position of enjoyment that justified the acquisition. Pure and simple monetization may be useful in certain cases, of course, but treating it as the default answer is precisely the kind of dogmatic limitation that this thesis strives to overcome.

This logic also serves for the control of unilateral alterations in themselves. The CDC does not look kindly on clauses and practices that authorize the supplier to modify on its own the content, the quality or the essential parameters of the performance after contracting<1><2>743</2></1>. The problem does not lie in every change considered in the abstract, but in the mutation imposed without effective participation of the consumer, without preservation of the balance of the relationship and without respect for the functional core of enjoyment. A relevant unilateral modification, when unanchored from restoration and from substantial preservation of use value, ceases to be simple management of the service and begins to approach structural abusiveness <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 655; p. 495-496])</4>.

This point connects directly to the theme of trust. In continuing relationships, the protection of trust is not theoretical perfume. It is the criterion that prevents the platform from treating the consumer as a hostage to an object whose function can be redefined at any moment for the exclusive benefit of the supplier<1><2>744</2></1>. In captive contracts, the so-called supervening <3>p. 655</3> “consensus” frequently amounts to no more than forced adherence to the new state of affairs, especially when the consumer is already invested in the relationship and depends on the ecosystem to continue enjoying what he acquired. Alterations that empty the utility, the quality or the material position of the consumer in the relationship may constitute, even under the appearance of continued acceptance, a form of de facto unilateral variation of the contract incompatible with good faith <4>Marques</4><5>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225; p. 1251; p. 1319-1320)</5>.

For this reason, functional value equivalence is a criterion of stability of the performance program, not a requirement of immobility of the object. It makes it possible to recognize the sophisticated obvious: continuous digital services change, but they cannot change in just any way; IOCs evolve, but they cannot be emptied under the label of evolution; platforms administer ecosystems, but they cannot use this administration to unilaterally transfer to the consumer the cost of relevant downgrades of enjoyment. The <1>standard</1> does not prevent the life of the service. It prevents the life of the service from being used as a screen for the material breach of what was functionally promised.

The example of updates that degrade accessibility and compatibility in software or firmware helps to visualize the structure of the problem. In these cases, no one seriously argues that every update is unlawful. What is argued is whether, under the pretext of improvement, the update relevantly impairs the use, performance or compatibility of goods still within their expected durability, without adequate information, without effective consent and without mitigating paths. The legal structure is the same in IOCs: an update, rebalancing or rule change is not illegitimate for existing, but may become unlawful when it substantially degrades the functional core of the acquisition without verifiable justification and without adequate restoration. The mutability of the ecosystem does not absolve the supplier of responsibility for preserving, in substantial terms, the utility that gave meaning to consumption.

On the methodological plane, the advantage of the <1>standard</1> is clear. It avoids both the extremism of “it changed, therefore it is unlawful” and the complacency of asserting that “change is inherent, so everything is lawful”. Contrary to such caricatures, it offers a finer criterion: did the alteration substantially preserve the functional, ecosystemic and, when relevant, symbolic core of enjoyment? Was there verifiable justification? Was there adequate restoration? If the answer is negative, mutability has ceased to be a legitimate attribute of the service and has turned into an <2>p. 656</2> instrument for emptying enjoyment, with its own consequences under the CDC regime <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 424])</4>.

This is what justifies asserting, with some firmness, that functional value equivalence is not just one more agreeable concept but rather the parameter of material lawfulness of alterations in IOCs. Without it, the supplier will always be able to hide behind the formal permanence of the object or the rhetoric of continuous innovation. With it, it becomes possible to ask what really matters: did the platform change the service while substantially preserving the functional value of what the consumer acquired, or did it use its position of governance to opportunistically downgrade, suppress or empty the promised enjoyment? It is precisely this question that functional value equivalence makes it possible to answer.

In continuing and structurally dependent relationships, consumer protection is not limited to the nominal preservation of the relationship or to the mere formal survival of the contracted object. What the system protects, in material terms, is a minimum level of stability of the performance program and of the trust legitimately built over the course of the relationship. The new relevance of the time factor in long-term captive relationships is reflected “in the imposition of a new level of maintenance of the relationship”, adding that, in this type of contract, the legitimate interest of the consumer is oriented toward the continuity of the relationship and, in principle, toward its renewal occurring “on the same terms and conditions as the initial policy” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1233)</2>. Legitimate expectations form the “minimum (objective) basis of the relationship, of the consumer contract”, so that, with these expectations excluded, “the imbalance of the relationship is flagrant” <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 292)</4>. Functional value equivalence thus operates as a criterion of the lawfulness of alterations in lasting relationships, prohibiting the suppression or degradation of the minimum basis of utility and trust that sustained the consumer's joining and remaining. <5>↩</5>

Technical term designating the numerical and statistical attributes (such as damage, resistance and speed) that parameterize the performance and effectiveness of an object or character. They constitute the logical basis of the functional utility of the IOC, being the main target of the unilateral modulations made by the platform under the justification of evolution or rebalancing of the service. <1>↩</1>

Functional value equivalence can be sustained as a consumer-law criterion of the lawfulness of alterations because liability for quality defects arises from the violation of a duty of adequacy, that is, of the quality of the product or service to serve the ends legitimately expected of it. The quality defect is not to be confused with absolute nonperformance, but corresponds to partial or imperfect performance, directed at satisfying the parties' interest in the performance of the contract itself <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 521])</2>. It follows that the nominal permanence of the object, of access or of the relationship is not enough, by itself, to rule out inadequacy. The quality defect arises from the absence of properties or characteristics that enable the performance to meet the ends legitimately expected by the consumer, and may even result from the violation of an accessory duty, provided this impairs, even partially, the utility of the product or service <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 523])</4>. In continuous and digitally governed consumer relationships, the mutation made by the platform is not lawful merely because something continues to exist; the parameter is whether what remains still serves, in a functionally equivalent way, the ends that legitimately justified the contracting. <5>↩</5>

The inadequacy of the performance, under the CDC regime, is not reduced to the physical nonexistence of the object or to its total suppression. Consumer-law dogmatics reaches situations in which the performance continues to exist formally or materially, but no longer corresponds, in legal terms, to the legitimately expected quality, functionality or conformity. The product may be considered legally unfit for failing to observe a regulatory presentation requirement, even though it meets immediate practical needs <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 328])</2>. The functional defect is a nonconformity that prevents or limits the function for which the good is intended, and may reach even irregularities of lesser apparent gravity related to details that frustrate the consumer's legitimate expectation <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 246])</4>. If the relevant enjoyment was downgraded, if the expected functionality was impaired or if the trust legitimately incorporated into the relationship was frustrated, consumer-law inadequacy has already set in. <5>↩</5>

The consumer's legitimate trust, in continuing relationships, projects itself onto the preservation of the expected utility of the contract over time. In long-term relationships, the permanence of the relationship has real legal value only if the performance remains capable of satisfying, at a minimally equivalent level, the purpose that justified the initial joining and sustained the continuity of the relationship. The theory of the relational contract contributes “to a new understanding of the trust awakened by the activity of suppliers and to the acceptance of a constant readaptation of long-term relationships so as not to frustrate the legitimate expectations of the parties, despite the limited will initially manifested.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 101)</2>. The material test of legitimate readaptation lies in whether the modification preserves the expected utility that the relationship promised to deliver to the consumer and in which he legitimately trusted. <3>↩</3>

The lawfulness of contractual mutations in prolonged relationships is not measured only by the formal permanence of the object nor by the abstract existence of a clause permitting alteration. In lasting relationships, change remains legally tolerable only when compatible with objective good faith, with the functional continuity of the performance and with the trust legitimately built in the course of execution. Objective good faith functions expressly as a yardstick for assessing lawfulness in the exercise of rights derived from legal transactions, including to set the limits of the exercise of termination in lasting contracts of continuing execution and to impose brakes on the <1>ius variandi</1> in specific cases <2>Martins-Costa</2><3>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 45)</3>. What proves legally relevant is the unfavorable and harmful surprise produced by unjustified hesitations, successive alterations or abrupt change of previously tolerated patterns, in rupture with the trust generated by the preceding conduct <4>Martins-Costa</4><5>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 401)</5>. A mutation that relevantly empties the promised enjoyment and breaks the contractual program concretely lived without sufficient restoration goes beyond the field of legitimate adaptation and enters that of the violation of trust. <6>↩</6>

In prolonged relationships, the lawfulness of alterations cannot be assessed only by the formal subsistence of the performance, because the relationship is not structured solely by the initial synallagma, but also by its functional continuity over time. Contractual balance is not limited to the moment of agreement, also corresponding to the “dynamic or functional synallagma”, that is, the one that accompanies the contractual relationship over the course of its duration <1>Martins-Costa</1><2>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 75)</2>. The transformations that affect the relationship during this iter must be brought back to the very structural and functional unity of the relationship <3>Martins-Costa</3><4>(Martins-Costa, 2018, p. 232)</4>. The relationship can bear changes only to the extent that they remain compatible with its concrete purpose and with the functional unity built in the contractual experience. If the mutation relevantly breaks this functional unity, downgrades the expected utility and empties the trust concretely built in the course of the relationship, the merely formal permanence of the relationship no longer serves as a sufficient criterion of lawfulness. <5>↩</5>

A relevant unilateral alteration of the performance must be read as a simultaneous problem of structural abusiveness and of material impairment of adequacy. Clauses that authorize the supplier to unilaterally modify the content or quality of the contract after its conclusion are abusive, precisely because they concentrate in the supplier the power to direct the relationship and reduce the consumer to a mere spectator of the course of the transaction <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 387])</2>. If unilateral alteration is already enough, in itself, to characterize abusiveness, this characteristic is aggravated when the content of the change results in the reduction or impairment of the consumer's interest in the performance <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 425])</4>. If the platform changes the game on its own in a way that preserves the shell, but empties the utility the consumer trusted to receive, there is a breach of legitimate expectation and legally relevant inadequacy. <5>↩</5>

The protection of the consumer's trust provides a direct basis for requiring substantial preservation of the utility enjoyed. The right to the maintenance of the originally contracted conditions derives from the application of good faith and from the binding effect of the offer, from which results the prohibition of unilateral alteration of the terms of the contract <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 424])</2>. The consumer makes his decision to contract in view of the advantages and qualities relating to the object or to the manner of contracting offered by the supplier, giving rise to the legal duty to maintain the offered conditions, in respect for the motives that led to the contract and for the contractual cause itself <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 424])</4>. In relationships of continued enjoyment, what must be preserved, or adequately restored, is the functional core of the advantages, qualities and utilities that motivated the contracting. Functional value equivalence is an unfolding of good faith, of the binding effect of the offer and of the protection of trust within the CDC. <5>↩</5>

Unilateral alteration clauses and practices are treated in the CDC from the direct perspective of contractual imbalance and abusiveness. Any modification of the consumer contract must observe bilaterality and the absence of abusive imposition, so that the clause that arms the supplier with the prerogative to innovate unilaterally in the relationship departs from contractual balance, its validity being undermined by Article 51, item XIII <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 655])</2>. The unilateral modification of adjustment indices or formulas amounts to an iniquitous, abusive and excessively disadvantageous imposition on the consumer, prohibited by the abusive clauses of Article 51 <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 495-496])</4>. Relevant unilateral alterations are legally problematic not because every change is prohibited in the abstract, but because the mutation imposed without effective participation of the consumer and without preservation of the balance of relevant enjoyment amounts to abusiveness and authorizes material restoration of the performance. <5>↩</5>

The control of unilateral modifications, in captive contracts, requires assessing whether the alteration materially empties the consumer's position in the continuing relationship, beyond the apparent form of the change. In relationships marked by practical dependence and strong preponderance of the supplier, the so-called supervening “consensus” frequently amounts to no more than forced adherence, constituting a rescission contrary to good faith and a fraud on the law for permitting the de facto unilateral variation of the content, the performances, the quality or the price <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1225)</2>. Clauses that authorize the supplier to unilaterally modify “the content of the contract or the quality of the contract” after its conclusion are abusive, as are practices that leave to its discretion the alteration of performances or of the price over time <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1251; p. 1319-1320)</4>. The control of the lawfulness of alterations must reach every modification that, although keeping the relationship standing on the nominal plane, corrodes the utility, the quality or the material position of the consumer built in the course of the relationship. <5>↩</5>

<1>6.3.3 </1>On the mechanisms appropriate to enabling procedures of open auditability and assessment of functional equivalence

In IOCs, open auditability and functional value equivalence only become legally useful when they can be converted into concrete mechanisms of controllability of supply. Without this, they remain <1>standards</1> that are correct in theory, but harmless in practice, especially in environments in which the platform concentrates architecture, records, criteria of alteration and means of proof. The problem, therefore, is not only to recognize that enjoyment is governed, but to determine how the consumer-law system can react when this governance becomes opaque, unilaterally reconfigures the acquired utility and further monopolizes the reconstruction of what happened. The answer does not require creating a new microsystem or importing an autonomous regulatory regime for platforms. It can be built from the combination of objective good faith, the duty of adequate information, relational cooperation, specific relief, production of documents and redistribution of the burden of proof already admitted in the CDC and the CPC <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</3><4><5>745</5></4> <6>Miragem</6><7>(Miragem, 2020, p. 856)</7><8><9>746</9></8>.

<1>p. 657</1> If the platform can alter, modulate, remove, recalibrate, sanction and reinterpret enjoyment on an ordinary basis, then legal control needs to shift from the abstraction of the “power to change” to the verifiability of what was changed, of how this was communicated and of the impacts it produced on the utility legitimately expected by the consumer. In other words, the law does not need to forbid every mutation of the service; it needs to prevent relevant mutations from being pushed onto the consumer as a fait accompli, without a reconstructible trail, without a minimally intelligible explanation and without a real possibility of challenge. It is at this point that open auditability and functional equivalence cease to be merely material criteria and come to require their own procedural instruments: qualified communication, preservation of evidence, production of records, expert examination delimited by functional impact and remedies oriented toward restoring enjoyment, and not only toward the later payment of losses and damages<2><3>747</3></2> <4>Bessa</4><5>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 111; p. 385; p. 783)</5>.

The first of these mechanisms is the duty of reasoning and qualified communication in relevant alterations. In continuous digital services, it is not enough for the platform to “publish an update”, “release a patch note” or bury the modification in layers of text, links or generic notices. When the change is capable of impacting the core of enjoyment of the IOC, good faith requires communication oriented to the essential, hierarchized and timed appropriately to the moment when the consumer can still understand the impact, react, decide and, if necessary, challenge. A relevant alteration cannot be communicated as noise or as a peripheral detail, because this turns mutability into a semiotic trap. The very relational logic of good faith prevents the supplier from imposing unnecessary or malicious expedients that make the exercise of the right a documentary <1>via crucis</1> or a scavenger hunt. If breaching the duty of cooperation and loyalty already means nonperformance, even if <2>p. 658</2> partial, then communication designed to neutralize the useful understanding of the change also violates the regime of the relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</4>.

This duty of qualified communication also prevents the platform from turning the consumer's silence, passivity or mere remaining in the environment into fictitious acceptance of relevant mutations. In continuing relationships, a substantial alteration of the performance cannot be implemented by a generic notice, a hidden cross-reference or a notification structured to go unnoticed and later be used as an alibi of consent. When the company modifies content, quality, parameters or relevant conditions of enjoyment, it must offer abundant, intelligible and timely information, precisely because the consumer is inserted in a relationship of practical dependence in which the cost of exit, adaptation or challenge is not neutral<1><2>748</2></1> <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</4>. The point is elementary, but it tends to be solemnly sabotaged by platform practice: if the change is important enough to affect enjoyment, it is important enough to be communicated in a way the consumer can understand without having to do digital archaeology.

The second mechanism is the preservation of minimum technical records as a condition of effective control. In IOCs, the supplier controls not only the object and the environment; it also controls the institutional memory of supply. It knows what was shown, when it was shown, how it was altered, which version was in force, which interface trail led to the contracting, which parameter was applied in a sanction, which transaction occurred and in what technical context. When all these elements remain under the platform's monopoly, the governance of the service also becomes governance of proof. For this reason, the minimum preservation of records ceases to be an administrative detail and becomes a condition of controllability. What is required here is not a total search of the system, but a minimum documentary core: history of relevant versions; essential records of alterations with functional impact; trails of consent and of the decision flow; history of relevant transactions; communications of change; and, when there is <1>enforcement</1>, basic records of the decision event, such as the category applied, the reason and the consequence<2><3>749</3></2> <4>Bessa</4><5>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 131; p. 145; p. 184)</5>.

<1>p. 659</1> This design is entirely compatible with the critique already developed of performative transparency. If the platform can appear to have informed without really making the information useful, it can also appear to have governed legitimately without preserving minimum trails that allow institutional reconstruction of what it did.

Open auditability is not limited to an abstract duty to “be transparent”; it requires a minimally documented regime of reconstruction of supply. The consumer does not need to know the total engineering of the system, but needs to be able to demonstrate — and protection bodies need to be able to verify — what occurred in a legally relevant way. Without this, the technical mutability of the service becomes an evidentiary safe-conduct, and the duty to inform degenerates into archival performance: a lot of paper for little verifiability.

The third mechanism is properly procedural: preservation of evidence, production of documents and dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof. When proof is born and remains under the platform's control, the procedural system cannot feign neutrality. The CPC already offers quite clear instruments to deal with this. Article 373, paragraph 1<1><2>750</2></1>, permits a different distribution of the burden of proof when there is excessive difficulty for one party to discharge the burden or greater ease for the other to produce proof of the contrary fact <3>Brasil</3><4>(Brasil, [2025]b)</4>. In disputes over IOCs, this is precisely the normal configuration: logs, interface trails, alteration histories, sanction criteria, internal support communications and relevant technical records are concentrated in the supplier. The dynamic redistribution of the burden, therefore, does not arise as extravagant judicial benevolence, but as a technically adequate response to the structural asymmetry of proof <5>Bessa</5><6>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 145; p. 184)</6>.

In the same vein, the regime for the production of a document or thing provided for in Articles 396 to 400 of the CPC offers the most direct path to operationalize open auditability. The judge may order the party to produce a document or thing in its possession (Article 396<1><2>751</2></1>), provided the request indicates, as completely as possible, the document or record sought, its evidentiary purpose and the circumstances showing that it is with the opposing <3>p. 660</3> party (Article 397<4><5>752</5></4>) <6>Brasil</6><7>(Brasil, [2025]b)</7>. This allows surgical requests, not procedural fishing expeditions.

Instead of generically requesting “all the data in the system”, the consumer may seek, for example, the history of relevant versions of a given item, the trail of screens displayed along the purchase path, the minimum records of the specific transaction, the content of the communication of alteration or the category and reason for the sanction applied. If the supplier denies possessing the document, Article 398<1><2>753</2></1> allows the requesting party to demonstrate by other means that the denial is untrue; if the refusal is unjustified, Article 400<3><4>754</4></3> authorizes the judge to admit as true the facts that the document would serve to prove <5>Brasil</5><6>(Brasil, [2025]b)</6>. In platform-related disputes, procedural guarantees satisfy the need to react to generic answers such as “we no longer have such information”, “this is internal-use data”, “this information is not accessible to the public” or “we are unable to reconstruct the procedure”.

This evidentiary arm connects directly with the duty of real clarification already recognized in consumer law. The supplier does not fulfill its role merely by throwing information into the environment; it also needs to demonstrate, when questioned, that it informed adequately, that it regularly exercised its power of alteration and that the impact produced was compatible with the promised performance. Demonstrating compliance with these duties forms part of its own burden of proof <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 412)</2>.

When there is greater risk without sufficiently conspicuous information, an informational defect or a relevant mutation whose intelligibility depends on data controlled by the company, it will fall to the company to demonstrate the nonexistence of the defect or nonconformity, and not to the consumer to prove in the dark what happened inside the environment he does not control <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 488)</2>. Without this adjustment, the platform becomes simultaneously master of the fact and of the process, concentrating in itself both control of the occurrence and control of the institutional means of its reconstruction.

<1>p. 661</1> The fourth mechanism is technical expert examination oriented to functional impact, and not to the total engineering of the ecosystem. When the controversy requires specialized examination, the expert examination need not and should not turn into an infinite audit of the platform, nor into a demand for full disclosure of source code, architecture or trade secret. Its object must be delimited by the legally relevant effects of supply: what changed, to what extent this affected the utility, the compatibility, the continuity, the ecosystemic position or the functional equivalence of the IOC. The expert examination comes in as a tool for closing the reconstruction, operating on minimum records, relevant versions, preserved trails and verifiable functional parameters. Thus, both absolute opacity and the fantasy of total transparency are avoided. The process does not need to become a complete autopsy of the system; it only needs to be able to answer, with method, the legally right question.

This delimitation is also important to reconcile the <1>standards</1> with the protection of software and with trade secrets. Open auditability is not oriented toward the unrestricted disclosure of the supplier's technical infrastructure, but toward minimum documentation and the verifiability of the legally relevant effects of supply. What is protected here is not the consumer's technological curiosity, but the institutional possibility of reconstructing alterations and impacts that affect his enjoyment. There is, therefore, compatibility between preserving secrecy and requiring verifiability. Trade secrecy may justify restraint in exposure; it cannot function as an absolute veto on reconstructing what the platform did when that doing has become legally contentious. Otherwise the business becomes peculiarly safe for the supplier, since it has authorization to change, harm its consumers, explain nothing and still invoke trade secrets as a kind of generalized excuse to avoid any possibility of being held liable. The model does not hold up.

The fifth mechanism concerns remedies and protection proper. Here the central point is that the operationalization of open auditability and functional equivalence should not automatically end in losses and damages as the default solution. The consumer-law microsystem prioritizes specific relief, measures capable of ensuring a practical result equivalent to performance and material restoration of the contracted utility <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 856; p. 897)</2>. In IOCs, this means that the <3>standards</3> need to guide remedies aimed at restoring the functional and, where appropriate, symbolic integrity of enjoyment. Among these remedies are reversal of a relevant alteration, re-performance, restoration or maintenance of access, preservation of history, restoration of ecosystemic or reputational attributes, equivalent functional substitution, mitigation through alternative versions, correction of parameters <4>p. 662</4> and proportional compensation when full restoration is not feasible<5><6>755</6></5> <7>Miragem</7><8>(Miragem, 2020, p. 529-530)</8>.

This orientation is coherent with the very logic of the regime of quality defects in the CDC. The system does not treat inadequacy only as an occasion to compensate; it treats it as an event that triggers duties to restore the utility enjoyed. If, on the classical plane, this already manifests itself in the priority given to replacing the product or service with another in perfect conditions of use, in IOCs the same rationale must be adapted to reconstitute the substantial utility of the digitally governed object. Instead of throwing everything into the monetary blender and calling it protection, it is argued that the remedy most faithful to the system is the one that gives back to the consumer, as far as possible, the legitimately expected enjoyment.

This remedial dimension also connects with specific enforcement and with the mandatory mechanisms of the microsystem itself. The integration between the CDC and collective redress allows the imposition of obligations to perform, correction protocols, maintenance of adequate supply, continuity of services and other measures capable of giving material effectiveness to consumer rights <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 111; p. 385; p. 783)</2>. When the dispute reveals a repeated pattern of opacity, abusive reconfiguration or unverifiable suppression of functional value, the response need not be limited to the individual case. It may take on a structural form: a duty to preserve minimum trails, to formalize qualified communication for relevant alterations, to organize intelligible challenge procedures, to maintain minimum functional impact reports or to adjust the supply regime to prevent repetition of the problem. This is especially important on platforms, where unlawfulness usually comes in batches, not as a single piece.

The sixth mechanism is coordinated institutional action. Without opening a parallel regulatory front, the subsection shows that open auditability and functional equivalence can also guide the action of protection bodies in platform markets. These <1>standards</1> offer a concrete criterion for adjustment agreements, recommendations, civil investigations and minimum governance requirements: functional impact reports on relevant alterations, protocols of verifiable transparency, preservation of essential records, comprehensible <2>p. 663</2> challenge procedures and minimum criteria of restoration in case of relevant degradation of enjoyment. First, the debate is prevented from remaining confined to the retail of the individual case. Second, the platform is prevented from continuing to operate under the fiction that each opaque reconfiguration is a mere technical detail and each conflict is just a little bad luck for the user.

All the mechanisms respond to the same requirement: to prevent the supplier's exclusive technical control from becoming a monopoly over the proof of the very unlawful act alleged. In IOCs, enjoyment is not given once and for all; it is continuously administered. If the platform also administers what can be seen, what can be remembered, what can be documented and what can be demonstrated, then the asymmetry ceases to be merely informational and becomes institutional. It is precisely to break this vicious circle that the subsection converts open auditability and functional equivalence into procedures: a duty to communicate adequately, a duty to preserve minimum records, a duty to produce relevant documentation, the possibility of functionally oriented expert examination, redistribution of the burden of proof and remedies of material restoration <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2> <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 131; p. 145)</4>.

For this reason, in IOCs, open auditability and functional equivalence do not operate on an object taken in abstraction, but on the concretely governed regime of enjoyment. Their proper field of application is the governance that conditions access, alteration, verifiability, challenge and restoration of what the consumer actually acquires and continues to enjoy. Without enabling mechanisms, the <1>standards</1> would be merely dogmatic good intentions. With them, they come to function as legal technology for the controllability of continuous supply. It is necessary to leave the plane of distant ideals to actually enter the terrain where the platform can be legally obliged to explain, show, preserve, restore and stop hiding behind its own black box.

The enabling of procedures of open auditability and assessment of functional equivalence is linked to minimum procedural duties derived from objective good faith, requiring the supplier to refrain from imposing unnecessary or malicious expedients that turn the exercise of the right into an endurance test. The relational structure offered to the consumer must make it possible, cooperatively, to understand relevant alterations, access essential information and challenge decisions without artificial barriers, since excessive difficulties that prevent the fulfillment of the main performance mean breach of duties of conduct under good faith: "to breach the duty of cooperation, of loyalty, means nonperformance, even if partial." <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1242)</2>. If the relationship is continuous, the supplier's duty is to make the path of change controllable, and not to hide the trail behind bureaucratic obstacles or hostile interfaces. <3>↩</3>

The consumer-law system prioritizes specific relief or measures capable of ensuring the practical result equivalent to the fulfillment of the obligation, admitting conversion into losses and damages only on a subsidiary basis <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 856])</2>. In continuous contractual relationships, this structure reinforces jurisdictional effectiveness in preventing undue terminations and guaranteeing the maintenance of the agreed utility <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 897])</4>. Open auditability and the assessment of functional equivalence therefore require mechanisms that make it possible to produce proof about the effects of alterations and to impose on the supplier the reestablishment or restoration of the promised functional utility. The consumer need not settle for residual monetary compensation after the sabotage of enjoyment, since the microsystem already admits remedies aimed at rebuilding the material integrity of supply. <5>↩</5>

Specific relief, continuity of supply and obligations to perform constitute internal instruments of the microsystem aimed at the concrete realization of consumer rights. In actions for the fulfillment of obligations, the discipline of specific enforcement takes on special importance, including with the imposition of daily fines, as a means of producing the material result owed and discouraging deliberate breach by economic calculation <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 111])</2>. Through the integration between the CDC and the Public Civil Action Law, mandatory and executive orders capable of providing adequate and effective protection are admissible, ensuring that services are supplied adequately and, if essential, continuously <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 385; 783])</4>. Faced with functional downgrading, the system admits the imposition of positive duties on the supplier to restore the utility of the contract, instead of reducing protection to a mere monetary settlement <5>ex </5> <6>post</6>. <7>↩</7>

Preserving the consumer's trust in the face of relevant modifications of the relationship requires qualified communication and effective cooperation, capable of allowing the impact on the performance to be assessed in good time. Significant alterations cannot be implemented through communications that are generic or structured to convert silence into fictitious acceptance, a practice considered abusive for authorizing the unilateral modification of the content or quality of performances after the conclusion of the contract <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</2>. Even when companies intend to use such mechanisms, they must ensure abundant information and a reasonable period for the consumer, failing which it constitutes exploitation of the passivity and practical dependence inherent in contracts of continuing execution <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1319-1320)</4>. <5>↩</5>

The effectiveness of consumer-law protection requires evidentiary cooperation and the production of elements, preventing whoever holds the records and the technical know-how from turning this advantage into a shield against legal control. Guided by the principle of procedural collaboration, the supplier bears the burden of proving the fulfillment of its duties, since each party must contribute the elements that can most easily be required of it, without prejudice to the reversal of the burden of proof <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 131])</2>. Facilitating defense in the CDC is part of the core of access to a just legal order, justifying the redistribution of the informational weight whenever the consumer's challenge is neutralized by technical opacity <3>Bessa</3><4>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 145; 184])</4>. Dynamic distribution and reversal of the burden of proof function as indispensable instruments of distributive justice in the face of the concentration of evidence on the supplier's side. <5>↩</5>

Material restoration in consumer law is oriented toward restoring the adequate performance, grounded in the user's interest in the very enjoyment of the contracted object. In the regime of quality defects, the priority given to replacing the product or service with another in perfect conditions of use reveals that adequate protection seeks the concrete recovery of the utility that motivated the contracting, and not merely the symbolic satisfaction of pecuniary compensation <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, [p. 529-530])</2>. In digital services and immaterial objects, this logic persists: when functional utility is downgraded or inadequately altered, the remedy most faithful to the system is the one aimed at reestablishing the performance through re-performance, reversal or delivery of an equivalent practical result. Auditability and functional equivalence must serve to guide remedies capable of giving back to the consumer the substantial utility legitimately expected. <3>↩</3>

The private governance of the IOC cannot be controlled only by the simplistic question about the abstract possibility of change. In platform ecosystems, changing is part of the very way of performing. The legal problem, therefore, does not lie in finding out whether the platform may alter the environment, but in establishing the criteria by which legitimate mutation is distinguished from mutation that breaks the balance of supply, degrades the promised enjoyment or makes the very possibility of control opaque. This shift is decisive because it prevents the controversy from being imprisoned between two equally bad extremes: on one side, the fantasy of the immobility of the digital object; on the other, the fantasy, symmetrically convenient to the supplier, that every ordinary mutation would be automatically legitimate because it derives from the “nature of the service”. In IOCs, mutability exists, but it does not hover above the Law.

After reconstructing semiotic vulnerability, the duty to inform in the key of adequacy, advertising as controllable production of expectation and abusiveness as a phenomenon that may reside in the entire arrangement of supply, it is no longer enough to assert generically that the platform must act with good faith, transparency and respect for the consumer. It is necessary to convert such requirements into operational criteria capable of guiding proof, attribution and remedy. The task is precisely to avoid this fate, offering <1>standards</1> capable of disciplining the legitimacy of platform architectures without depending either on the civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good or on the scattered hunt for isolated clauses.

The first difficulty faced by the section stems from the object itself. In continuous digital services, a large part of the controversies does not arise from abrupt and conspicuous suppression, but from progressive alterations, functional reconfigurations, interface changes, redefinitions of equivalence, visibility adjustments, <1>nerfs</1>, <2>resets</2>, rule migrations and other moves that, taken in isolation, may seem trivial, but that, together or with sufficient intensity, restructure the acquired experience. The consumer remains formally “inside” the ecosystem, still has the account, still sees the object, can still access the platform. Even so, the utility enjoyed may be substantially downgraded, and the ability to prove this downgrading may be simultaneously eroded by the very way the environment is administered. It is precisely against this combination of normalized mutability and operational opacity that the section proposes two complementary criteria.

<1>p. 636</1> The first of them is open auditability. The name must be read carefully so as not to produce misunderstanding. It is not a matter of requiring the opening of code, a total search of the infrastructure, full publicity of internal systems or theatrical laboratory transparency. Open auditability works on a more sober and more legal plane, since it designates the requirement of minimum institutional verifiability of supply. In other words, the platform cannot claim to alter the regime of enjoyment and, at the same time, keep in absolute secrecy what it actually altered, when it altered, why it altered, what relevant effects the change produces and which records allow the episode to be reconstructed in case of conflict. The <2>standard</2> does not require exposure of trade secrets as a purifying fetish. It does require a demonstrable minimum capable of preventing information, good faith and transparency from turning into empty performances.

Open auditability thus arises as a direct response to the functional opacity typical of IOCs. If the supplier controls the architecture, the criteria of alteration, the relevant logs, the timing of the change and the very means by which the modification will be perceived, it concentrates not only power of reconfiguration, but also power to narrate unilaterally what occurred. The legal risk there is obvious: without minimum trails, without minimally reconstructible reasoning and without the possibility of confronting promise and mutation, the consumer is reduced to the ridiculous position of feeling that he lost something important, but being unable to demonstrate institutionally what he lost, how he lost it, or why the loss exceeds the trivial annoyance inherent to networked life. Open auditability prevents exactly this erosion of control. It requires that the platform environment remain, at least to a minimum degree, reconstitutable.

This has quite concrete consequences. Open auditability extends to communications of alteration, history of relevant versions, confirmation screens, change notices, transaction records, logs sufficient to trace materially relevant interventions, minimum documentation of the supply flow and minimally intelligible explanation of the criteria invoked for relevant reconfigurations. It is neither necessary nor desirable to turn the supplier into a fully transparent oracle. What is required is something simpler and more serious: that the platform cannot benefit legally from the very opacity it produces. In terms of proof, this means that the supply regime needs to be institutionally reconstructible. In terms of legitimacy, it means that important mutations cannot rest only on the platform's naked authority. In terms of remedy, it means that the absence of trails and verifiability ceases to be an operational detail and becomes part of the unlawful act itself.

<1>p. 637</1> The second <2>standard</2> is functional value equivalence. If open auditability controls the verifiability of the change, functional value equivalence controls the substance of the enjoyment preserved or degraded by the change. The core of the idea is simple, though dogmatically powerful: in IOCs, the integrity of what was acquired cannot be measured only by the nominal survival of the object nor by the formal permanence of access. The fact that something continues to exist inside the account, remains technically accessible or continues to bear the same name is not enough, by itself, to demonstrate that the acquisition was preserved in its legally relevant value. In a mutable environment, what matters is the functional equivalence of enjoyment, that is, the substantial preservation of the practical utility and the sense of use that justified consumption.

This criterion is necessary because the platform supplier tends to operate with a very comfortable defense: nothing was taken away, everything merely “evolved”; nothing was suppressed, merely “rebalanced”; nothing was lost, merely “readjusted to the ecosystem”. Functional value equivalence prevents this managerial vocabulary from serving as a free pass for relevant downgrading of the experience consumed. What is asked, from it, is not whether the object is still there in a nominal sense, but whether the change preserves, to a legally acceptable extent, the set of functions, advantages, possibilities of use, practical value and symbolic density that made up the legitimately expected enjoyment. When this equivalence is relevantly broken, the mutation ceases to be a simple ordinary variation of the service and begins to touch the very core of the acquisition.

This <1>standard</1> is particularly useful because it escapes two traps. The first is the temptation to reduce every conflict to proprietary language, as if only a strong notion of ownership could protect the consumer against unilateral alterations. The section refuses this shortcut. It is not necessary to demonstrate full dominion over the object to maintain that the acquired enjoyment cannot be arbitrarily downgraded. The second trap is the trivialization of mutability as a supposedly natural trait of digital services, an argument that usually serves as technological varnish for opportunistic changes. Functional value equivalence allows, precisely, a much more robust intermediate position: it is recognized that the platform may alter, but it is required that the alteration preserve, in substantial terms, the functional value of the acquired experience or, failing that, open room for restoration, correction, revision or another adequate remedy.

The force of the criterion appears clearly in cases such as removals of relevant functionalities, nerfs that empty acquired utility, interface changes that disorganize ordinary use, redefinitions of rules that downgrade the equivalence of what was promised, <1>p. 638</1> alterations of currency or internal purchasing power, mutations in progression systems, reclassifications of rarity, erasure or compression of inventories, and changes in visibility patterns that affect the consumer's position in the ecosystem. In all these cases, the decisive question should not be whether the platform continued to offer “something” with the same label. The correct question is whether the thing legally acquired, as a position of enjoyment in a governed environment, retains sufficient functional equivalence with what was the object of the consumer's expectation, trust and investment.

It is important to note that functional value equivalence does not freeze the ecosystem. It does not require absolute identity between before and after, nor does it prohibit rebalancings, adjustments, corrections or evolutions of the environment. What it prevents is the use of mutability as a screen for the opportunistic destruction of value. The supplier is not obliged to fossilize the service, but neither may it take refuge in the idea of permanent evolution to legitimize any relevant reduction of the utility enjoyed. Instead of a simplistic opposition between immobility and total sovereignty of the platform, the <1>standard</1> introduces a more sophisticated test of legitimacy: the change may occur, provided it remains within margins compatible with the substantial preservation of enjoyment or is accompanied by adequate justification, verifiable transparency and fitting restoration when equivalence is broken.

It is there that the two criteria meet. Open auditability and functional value equivalence are not parallel <1>standards</1> that march without touching. They presuppose each other. Without auditability, functional equivalence is difficult to demonstrate, because the consumer cannot reconstruct what was altered, to what extent, with what motivation and at what moment. Without functional equivalence, auditability runs the risk of becoming transparency without material density, that is, a simple capacity to narrate changes without a criterion to assess their substantive legitimacy. One <2>standard</2> controls the how of the mutation; the other, the how much and the what of the mutation. One prevents institutional opacity; the other prevents functional downgrading disguised as ordinary management. Together, they offer something the debate lacked: a decision grammar capable of disciplining the legitimacy of platform architecture.

This complementarity makes it possible to reorganize the central question of controversies in IOCs. One no longer asks, in an impoverished way, whether or not the platform has the right to alter. One asks whether the alteration was accompanied by minimum conditions of verifiability and whether it preserved, in a substantially acceptable way, the functional equivalence of the acquired enjoyment. When one of these conditions fails, the legitimacy of the change already becomes legally suspect. When both fail at the same time, the case comes strongly close to a defect <1>p. 639</1> of supply, an abusive practice, a breach of trust or even an architecture of structural opacity incompatible with the consumer-law regime. The section, thus, does not turn every alteration into an unlawful act. It only refuses to let alteration become an automatic alibi for irresponsibility.

Semiotic vulnerability had shown that the platform controls the means by which the consumer understands, compares and proves his own enjoyment. The duty of information, read in the key of adequacy, had shown that volume and performative transparency are not enough. Advertising, treated as market semiotics, had revealed how expectation is curated in advance and is legally binding. Hypercuratorial anticipation had demonstrated that architecture, interface and platform dynamics operate together on the decision. Now, all this needs to be converted into a criterion of legitimacy for ordinary mutations of supply. That is exactly the role of open auditability and functional value equivalence.

Under such <1>standards</1>, there no longer remain only bad dogmatic exits. It is no longer necessary to reduce the conflict to a civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good, which would be narrow for governed consumption. Nor is there a need to remain trapped in the microscopic analysis of isolated clauses, as if the platform only produced unlawfulness through badly drafted contractual sentences. The focus comes to rest on the architecture of supply and on the material controllability of its mutations. In governed ecosystems, the relevant unlawful act is often not in a heroically villainous clause, but in the way the environment changes, justifies itself poorly, erases traces and preserves only the formal appearance of continuity.

When the controversy involves removals, rule alterations, interface changes, ecosystem rebalancings, compression of functionalities, redefinitions of equivalence or reconfigurations of value, the interpreter will have two central tests at hand. First, was there minimum institutional verifiability of the change, with reasoning, timing, effects and trails for reconstructing supply? Second, did the alteration preserve sufficient functional equivalence with the legitimately acquired enjoyment, or did it relevantly downgrade the practical and symbolic core of the object? From there, it already becomes possible to discipline proof, calibrate claims, structure remedies and control the privatist narrative according to which everything that occurs within the platform would be merely the neutral exercise of its freedom of management.
