Section 6.4.1 · pp. 665 to 669
<1>6.4.1 </1>On the unlawful act of abusive teleology: design defect and abusive practice

Abusive teleology designates, under the CDC regime, a qualified form of unlawfulness in which the exploitation of vulnerability does not appear as an episodic deviation in the functioning of the service, but as a purpose incorporated into its very program of operation. In continuous digital services, the legal problem is no longer limited to identifying a one-off error, an isolated communication failure or a singularly excessive clause. What must be controlled is the functional design of supply when it comes to organize, in a stable way, defective understanding, hindered reversibility, degradable enjoyment and structurally weakened challenge. Architecture, in this context, does not remain outside the performance. It is part of the very way in which utility is produced, maintained, restricted and made intelligible to the consumer.

It is precisely for this reason that the false dilemma between a defect in the product and a failure of governance must be rejected. In the IOC regime, immaterial product and governed environment are not opposed as independent layers. Enjoyment only becomes legally consumable through the governance that organizes it. When this governance is designed to stabilize asymmetries <1>p. 666</1> of understanding, of reversal, of proof and of tolerance to loss, the problem may be described, at the same time, as a defect in the supply regime and as a relevant degradation of the enjoyment of the object consumed. There is no competition between the two readings. There is complementarity. The same dysfunction appears, on one side, as a design defect in the mode of performance and, on the other, as a functional or symbolic downgrading of the utility promised to the consumer.

In this key, abusive teleology is not to be confused with a merely harsh business choice, with debatable design or with architecture that is simply efficient for the supplier. The category is justified only when the exploitative effect derives from the very design of the flow and of governance, when the mechanism presents itself as a stable and replicable pattern of functioning and when this pattern relevantly affects the consumer's practical autonomy and the integrity of enjoyment. The unlawful act does not arise, therefore, from a singular episode that can be treated as an accident. It arises when defaults, frictions, manufactured urgencies, hostile cancellation routes, elastic equivalences, sanction regimes or evidentiary arrangements function together as a method of exploitation. Abusiveness ceases to be a mere accident of execution and comes to reside in the program that organizes execution.

This formulation is not a license for judicial impressionism or abstract moralization of the digital environment. On the contrary, it functions as a technique of dogmatic containment. The category only makes sense because it allows repeated functional patterns to be treated as legally attributable units, instead of dissolving them into a collection of disconnected micro-events. Dogmatics does not operate by infinite reproduction of the empirical, but by bringing functionally similar occurrences back to a unitary normative frame, capable of guiding decision and legal consequence <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 99; p. 312-313])</2><3><4>756</4></3>. When the service repeats, with functional coherence, mechanisms for capturing choice, for making loss opaque and for <5>p. 667</5> demobilizing challenge, attributing the program is no longer rhetorical exaggeration. It is the technically adequate way of apprehending the unlawful act.

The same logic applies to the stability of the <1>standard</1>. Abusive teleology does not derive from an artificial aggregation of heterogeneous facts, but from the functional similarity between occurrences that reveal a common rationale of exploitation. Legal reasoning does not need to reproduce the case in its full empirical extent to treat it adequately; it abstracts, synthesizes and formulates a decision rule from a recognizable pattern <2>Jr.</2><3>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 52; p. 337])</3><4><5>757</5></4>. That is exactly what the category does here. It prevents the system from treating stable architectural exploitation as a mere sum of small isolated annoyances, each apparently trivial, but all functionally articulated for the benefit of the same program.

This framing also requires recognizing that abusiveness cannot remain confined to the atomized reading of isolated clauses. In platform-governed consumer relationships, legal control needs to reach the global logic of organization of the relationship, the distribution of frictions, facilities, barriers, opacities and asymmetries within supply. Abusiveness, therefore, is not measured only by the contractual sentence taken alone, but by the design of the contract and of the performance seen as a dynamic totality. Good faith and balance operate precisely on this plane, making it possible to identify abuse when contractual or procedural engineering concentrates excessive unilaterality and significant imbalance to the detriment of the consumer <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 163; p. 291)</2><3><4>758</4></3>. In continuous <5>p. 668</5> digital services, this means that decision flow, reversal architecture, distribution of noise, zones of opacity and the design of challenge already belong to the field of the consumer-law unlawful act.

For this reason, abusive teleology may operate, depending on the structure of the case, as a design defect in supply and as an abusive practice. As a design defect, it appears when the service is born already architected to produce asymmetry as a method, downgrading in advance intelligibility, reversibility and the minimum stability of enjoyment. As an abusive practice, it manifests itself when the everyday governance of the ecosystem repeatedly and predictably exploits the consumer's factual and semiotic vulnerability, administering urgency, scarcity, exit cost, informational noise or difficulty of proof for its own benefit. In borderline cases, the same rationale may further approach the figure of the safety defect of the service, when the program of functioning produces relevant risk or actual harm to reference legal interests, including those linked to personal integrity, biographical continuity and symbolic identity.

This qualification does not depend on proving the supplier's intimate psychological intention, as if the unlawful act required a subjective confession of malice. The focus falls on the functional purpose of the arrangement. What matters is how the program operates, what asymmetries it stabilizes and in what way it organizes the expected behavior of the consumer. Exploitation may be incorporated into the design even when business discourse presents it as simple technical neutrality, operational inevitability or a natural consequence of the service. In dogmatic terms, this suffices. The rationale of the program is legally more important than the benevolent self-description the platform gives of itself.

It is here that the notion of the barrier clause gains special value. Abusiveness manifests itself not only when the supplier frontally restricts a right, but also when it organizes the relationship to hinder, delay or discourage the exercise of that right through multiple steps, unnecessary requirements, artificial frictions and procedural increase in the cost of the consumer's reaction. When performance or reversal only become possible after excessively costly trails, without plausible justification, the very form of organization of the relationship already functions as a device for containing the consumer's claim. The CDC does not need to wait for a scandalous text to react. It is enough that the contractual or procedural structure operates as a mechanism of substantial imbalance, <1>p. 669</1> unjustifiably hindering the consumer's access to what would ordinarily be owed to him <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</3><4><5>759</5></4>.

With this, the unlawful act of abusive teleology gains more precise contours. It does not name every bad experience, every consumer frustration or every unfavorable alteration made on a platform. It names cases in which the architecture of the service was conceived or came to be administered so as to structurally exploit the consumer's vulnerability, turning opacity, friction, difficulty of reversal, capture of expectation and concentration of proof into ordinary elements of the performance. Its object is not the interface taken as aesthetics, but the functional organization of enjoyment. Its point of application is not the isolated anecdote, but the pattern. Its criterion is not cultural indignation at design, but the verifiability that the program operates against real understanding of the essential, against practicable reversibility, against intelligible challenge and against minimally loyal stability of the acquired enjoyment.

When the program of the service comes to operate in these terms, the CDC is not facing disconnected micro-incidents, but a mode of supply that is legally controllable in itself. The qualification of the unlawful act may then open, depending on the case, the door of the design defect, of the abusive practice, of the abusive clause that shields this program or, in aggravated cases, of the safety defect of the service. From there, the discussion ceases to revolve around the impoverished question of whether the platform “can or cannot change” and comes to bear on what really matters: whether the design of supply was organized in a way compatible with good faith, balance, auditability, functional equivalence and a real possibility of reaction by the consumer. When the answer is negative, abusive teleology ceases to be a theoretical hypothesis and becomes a technical category for attributing the exploitative program itself.

The formulation of the unlawful act of abusive teleology depends on recognizing that dogmatics can treat repeated functional patterns as legally attributable units, instead of dissolving them into disconnected micro-events. It is not a matter of moralizing the design of the service or of producing a sociological denunciation of the environment, but of verifying whether there is a program of functioning stable enough to receive unitary qualification. Ferraz Jr. offers a basis for this operation by showing that dogmatics apprehends social phenomena as "normed sets", that is, as units endowed with organization and structure, and not as dispersed empirical facts <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 99])</2>. It is in this key that abusive teleology can be treated as a technical category of attribution: legal relevance does not derive from the simple sum of isolated episodes, but from the possibility of bringing them back to a coherent functional pattern of exploitation. In addition, the author observes that, from the legal angle, the decisive question is not the brute causality of the event, but the normative attribution of consequences to legally qualified conduct <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312-313])</4>. The problem, here, is not only to demonstrate the fragmentary existence of acts of inducement, capture or opacity, but to know whether, legally, they compose a unitary program of abusive supply. <5>↩</5>

The stabilization of abusive teleology as a dogmatic category also rests on the proper form of legal deciding, which is not limited to collecting empirical occurrences, but reconstructs the case by synthesis, abstraction and controlled generalization. Ferraz Jr. observes that the jurist's work does not consist in reproducing cases "in their full extent", but in abstracting them, contrasting reasons and broadening the problem "in such a way that we can obtain from it a general rule that decides the case and serves for others" <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 52])</2>. This dispels the objection that abusive teleology would depend on an artificial aggregation of heterogeneous facts. On the contrary, when multiple occurrences reveal sufficient functional similarity, bringing them back to a unitary frame corresponds to the very normal mode of operation of dogmatics. The same reasoning sustains the formation of legal standards by similarity, including with support in decisions and examples, as the author records in mentioning the constitution of "legal standards" by the "principle of similarity" <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 337])</4>. Abusive teleology, thus, does not appear as a loose metaphor, but as a technical framing aimed at giving unitary treatment to a repeated pattern of architectural exploitation. <5>↩</5>

Within the CDC, the assessment of abusiveness cannot remain confined to the atomized reading of isolated clauses, as if the contract were merely a mosaic of legally autonomous sentences. The mode of organization of the contractual relationship — its global design, its internal logic of functioning, the distribution of frictions, facilities, reversals, informational burdens and points of opacity — is part of the very object of legal control. Marques offers a decisive basis for this reading by asserting that the interpreter's activity in identifying abusiveness must concentrate on a “dynamic and total view of contracts”, so that abusiveness is not observed in the isolated reading of the clause, but “in the reading of the whole of the contract, in the function of the clause in the contract as drafted, in the repercussion of the clause in that kind of contract” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 163)</2>. The author reinforces that, under the influence of good faith, abuse can also be identified in the “excessive unilaterality or unreasonable imbalance of the contractual engineering”, the “significant imbalance of rights and duties, to the detriment of the consumer, in the contractual relationship seen as a whole” being an indication of abuse <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 291)</4>. This authorizes treating architecture, decision flow and opacity as legally relevant elements of the performance itself. <5>↩</5>

Objective good faith and contractual balance also operate as direct limits on the creation of contractual or procedural structures designed to unilaterally favor the supplier. In consumer matters, it is not only the declaratory content of the clause that may be abusive, but also the way the relationship is organized to hinder, delay or discourage the exercise of the consumer's rights. Marques is precise in stating that the attempt to prevent performance may be directed at the supplier's own performance, when the contract makes it enforceable only after “certain and multiple authorizations, papers, proofs, without plausible justification, merely to hinder and discourage the consumer from asserting his own (and main) claim.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</2>. Claudia Lima Marques shows that the “barrier clause” is contrary to Article 51, item IV, of the CDC, precisely because it substantially unbalances the contractual relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1236)</4>. Applied to the unlawful act of abusive teleology, this reasoning makes it possible to control entire procedural arrangements conceived to produce asymmetric friction, increase the cost of reversal and demobilize challenge. <5>↩</5>

<1>6.4.2 </1>On the techniques of capture by scarcity, risk and dependence

<1>p. 670</1> The techniques of capture by scarcity, risk and dependence are of interest here neither as a moral catalog of “aggressive strategies” nor as a sociological inventory of engagement mechanisms. Their interest is dogmatic and evidentiary. In IOC ecosystems, exploitation rarely presents itself in the clean form of a scandalous clause or of an advertisement that is false in isolation. It tends to emerge as a program of functioning, that is, as an articulation between multiple mechanisms that compress reflection time, reorganize expectation, increase exit cost, hinder reversal and make enjoyment progressively dependent on the very environment that governs it. What is sought, then, is a controllable vocabulary for recognizing recurring patterns of capture, without psychologizing the consumer and without dissolving the problem into vague impressions about <2>design</2>.

This vocabulary is necessary precisely because exploitation, in continuous digital services, usually operates by accumulation. The consumer is rarely constrained by a single expedient. What occurs, more frequently, is the combination of staged scarcity, manufactured urgency, promise of progression, diffuse threat of loss, gradual downgrades of utility and symbolic anchoring of permanence. Seen in isolation, these elements may seem trivial, tolerable or even inherent to the ecosystem. Considered together, they reveal a clearer rationale of capture of choice and of administration of tolerance to harm. It is for this reason that atomization must be avoided. The exploitative program does not disappear just because it is distributed in small repeated incidences.

The first family of these techniques is that of artificial scarcity and manufactured urgency. Its mechanism is well known. Short windows, accelerated rotation of offers, countdown timers, “limited editions”, ephemeral events and temporary benefits are used to shift the decision from the field of rational comparison to that of reactive response. The legally relevant effect lies not only in making the purchase more attractive, but in deliberately compressing reflection time and inducing hasty consent, often when essential information remains hidden, dispersed or hierarchically downgraded. The problem is not the isolated use of temporality in the market, but its articulation with opacity and with the practical impossibility of comparison. The minimum sign of proof, here, does not depend on intuition about manipulation. It appears in time-remaining screens, in a history of repeated temporary campaigns, in programmed rotation of offers and in the very visual architecture that anticipates benefit and postpones relevant conditions.

The second family is that of temporal pressure through event structures and cycles of promise. The mechanism ceases to operate only through one-off rarity and comes to organize a directed sequence of anticipation, purchase, partial delivery, frustration and repurchase. Teasers, pre-sales, <1>p. 671</1> conditioned progressions, passes, serialized rewards and temporary goals build a trajectory in which value ceases to reside only in the object and comes to reside in the cost of “falling behind”. The relevant legal effect is the conversion of enjoyment into a directed path, in which giving up ceases to mean a mere interruption of consumption and comes to represent loss of accumulated value, regression of position and discontinuity of an expectation already installed. In continuing relationships, this dynamic gains special relevance because the consumer finds himself progressively more captive to the maintenance of the relationship and less free to resist new impositions by the supplier, which renews its power of influence precisely through the continuity of the relationship <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</3><4><5>760</5></4>. The minimum sign of proof emerges in progression structures, event rules, time requirements, modifications introduced mid-cycle and comparison between the initial promise and the actual delivery along the trajectory.

This logic may acquire additional gravity when the ecosystem is articulated with audiences especially exposed to the pressure of permanence and to the repeated promise of reward. In electronic game environments, the prolonged maintenance of engagement through new content, continuous development of the character and appeal to collective dynamics reinforces commitment to permanence and broadens tolerance to opaque retention structures. The combination of promise of progression, group belonging and marketing integrated into the play environment shows that capture does not operate only on the abstract individual, but may radiate effects onto children, adolescents and the family unit itself <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 19; p. 10-11; p. 17)</2><3><4>761</4></3>. This does not shift the axis of the subsection, but confirms that these techniques have sufficient materiality to exceed ordinary commercial persuasion.

<1>p. 672</1> The third family is that of the manufacture of risk and the permanent threat of loss. Here the mechanism depends not so much on the promise of gain as on the continuous administration of the possibility of loss. Programmed expiry, unilateral discontinuation, opaque banning, functional downgrades, loss of access to account or inventory, removals without a verifiable trail and unintelligible challenge regimes compose an environment in which trust is replaced by vigilance. The consumer ceases to choose in a space of minimum stability and comes to consume under a diffuse threat of deterioration, of sanction or of partial disappearance of what already makes up his position of enjoyment. The relevant legal effect lies precisely in this replacement of trust by discipline. Pressure ceases to be a mere psychological datum and becomes part of the legally relevant relational framework itself, because the supplier exercises its power in an environment in which the continuity of the relationship becomes a good in itself for the consumer and the threat of rupture or impoverishment of this continuity comes to operate as a method of subjection <2>Marques</2><3>(Marques, 2016, p. 285-286)</3><4><5>762</5></4>. The minimum sign of proof appears in applied policies, sanction communications, absence of verifiable reasoning, decisional inconsistencies and concentration of evidentiary trails in the supplier, which connects this family directly to the problem of open auditability.

The fourth family is that of the programmed degradation of use value and the downgrading of equivalence. Its mechanism is not mere change, but oriented change. Nerfs, reconfigurations, balancing adjustments, gradual suppressions of function, shifts of utility to new layers of acquisition and ordinary redefinitions of equivalence operate as techniques of extraction by erosion. The object does not leave the scene completely. It remains there, but worse, weaker, less central, less useful or less equivalent to what justified the acquisition. The relevant legal effect lies in the violation of the legitimate expectation of continued enjoyment. The consumer does not lose merely “a feature”; he loses functional substance of what he bought and is frequently pushed to seek substitutes within the same ecosystem. The minimum sign of proof requires functional comparison between before and after, examination of relevant versions, identification of the core of utility affected and assessment of the object's role in the experience, exactly as the standard of functional value equivalence already requires. Legal <1>p. 673</1> relevance, here, does not depend on total suppression, but on relevant and repeated erosion of enjoyment.

The fifth family is that of existential captivity and identity or social dependence. Here capture is anchored in the symbolic value produced by the system itself. Inventories, titles, history, <1>ranking</1>, rarities, emblems, status signs and marks of trajectory function as ties between the IOC and the consumer's social position in the ecosystem. The relevant legal effect is evident. The loss or degradation of the object ceases to operate only as a patrimonial reduction and comes to bear on belonging, recognition, memory of participation and symbolic identity, in the terms already set for the reference legal interests. The minimum sign of proof does not lie in a subjective account of sadness or frustration, but in the objective demonstration of how the system itself attributes social value to the object, through internal markers, visibility, participation requirements, access restrictions and reputational effects. When the environment attributes this value in an institutionalized way, it also institutionalizes the exit cost and raises the consumer's tolerance to capture.

This fifth family also helps to understand why certain retention and reward techniques cannot be read merely as innocent “engagement” tactics. In contexts of strong dependence on permanence, the cycles of challenge, reward and progression may intensify ties of permanence to a degree that goes beyond mere playful prolongation and comes to affect the user more deeply and, in sensitive situations, the family environment itself. The legal interest here is not to pathologize every intense relationship with the game, but to recognize that the dynamic of retention and reward may function as an objective mechanism for raising the exit cost and broadening dependence on the continuity of the relationship <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 20; p. 21; p. 23-24)</2><3><4>763</4></3>. The usefulness of this observation, in this item, is only to reinforce that dependence and capture are not metaphorical abstractions when the very design of the ecosystem organizes permanence as a socially charged necessity.

Considered together, these five families show that abusive teleology need not appear as a single, dramatic and conspicuous gesture. It may manifest itself through <1>p. 674</1> the accumulation of smaller incidences, each of low perceptibility when isolated, but all converging on the same functional result: compressing the consumer's practical freedom, increasing his tolerance to loss, hindering comparison, raising the exit cost and turning the continuity of the relationship into an instrument of extraction. For this reason, the vocabulary proposed here is predominantly descriptive-operational. Its role is not yet to close the definitive dogmatic qualification, but to make visible the exploitative program in its recurring forms of manifestation.

The internal consequence of the subsection is, then, quite precise. Scarcity, urgency, serialized promise, threat of loss, functional erosion and symbolic dependence are not unlawful for existing in the abstract nor for appearing in isolation. They become teleologically abusive when they operate in combination with opacity and permanent asymmetry, in a stable and replicable pattern, orienting enjoyment toward ends incompatible with good faith, balance and controllability of supply. Seen in this way, they produce fragmentary injuries that may seem small when examined separately, but that, reconstructed together, reveal economically relevant extraction and progressive reconfiguration of the consumer's position in the ecosystem. What is prepared, from here on, is not a category competing with abusive teleology, but the functional repertoire through which it becomes recognizable before being explicitly brought back to the framing doors of the CDC.

Capture techniques founded on scarcity, risk and dependence constitute legally relevant forms of exploitation of consumer vulnerability in continuing contractual relationships, taking advantage of established ties and of the user's practical need for permanence to broaden the supplier's power of imposition. Certain services and complex long-term relationships bind the consumer in such a way that he becomes dependent on the maintenance of the contractual relationship itself, on pain of seeing frustrated the expectations that led him to join and remain in the relationship: such relationships “bind the consumer in such a way that, over the years of duration of the complex contractual relationship, he becomes a 'captive' client of that supplier or chain of suppliers, becoming dependent even on the maintenance of that contractual relationship or he will see all his expectations frustrated.” <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</2>. This dependence reduces the consumer's real capacity to resist new impositions, guaranteeing the supplier a “power of imposition” constantly renewed over the course of the long-term obligation <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 109)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Capture techniques based on scarcity, dependence and pressure of permanence may acquire even greater gravity when they bear on children, adolescents and family dynamics mediated by the platform. In ecosystems such as <1>Fortnite</1>, the structure of the game aims to keep players connected for long periods through the continuous promise of new content, characters and game modes, a strategy that “generates long-term expectation among players and commitment to the development of the user's character” <2>Torres</2><3>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 19)</3>. The attraction of children is reinforced by partnerships with celebrities and brands, turning the play environment into a space of recurring stimulus to consumption, while the multiplayer logic “creates a team spirit forcing the player to continue in the game to help the other players” <4>Torres</4><5>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 10-11, 17)</5>. <6>↩</6>

The pressure exerted on the consumer in lasting contractual relationships forms part of the legally relevant relational framework for assessing good faith and abusiveness, ceasing to be a merely psychological or accidental datum. In contracts for increasingly essential services, “pressure” takes on growing relevance in resolving contractual conflicts, such that the exercise of certain rights by the professional in a position of power may constitute abuse of right or an act contrary to the good faith required in legal dealings, this structural-social factor of pressure having new legal relevance in captive relationships <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 285)</2>. The legitimate interest of the consumer is directed to the continuity of the contractual relationship, while pressure may lie in the sales method itself, in marketing or in the object of the contract, being reflected in the final engineering of the relationship <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 285-286)</4>. <5>↩</5>

Engagement and retention techniques in electronic games may intensify the dependence and exposure of the family unit itself, going beyond the prolongation of playful engagement. The dynamic of challenges and rewards may prevent children and adolescents from facing stress factors, “creating a vicious cycle of anxiety and depression” <1>Torres</1><2>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 20)</2>. This loss of control is linked to the “neural circuit established in the face of the reward provided”, similar to the functioning of brain reward systems in chemical dependencies <3>Torres</3><4>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 21)</4>. The effects radiate onto the family, generating expenses with treatments, requiring greater attention from those responsible and interfering with family income <5>Torres</5><6>(Azevedo; Torres, 2023, p. 23-24)</6>. <7>↩</7>

<1>6.4.3 </1>On framing in quality defects, abusive clauses and abusive practices

Framing abusive teleology within the categories of the CDC requires sufficient precision to avoid two symmetrical errors. The first would be to dilute the exploitative program into atomized episodes, as if each manifestation exhausted its meaning in an isolated occurrence and the architecture of capture disappeared in the sum of small facts. The second would be to turn abusive teleology itself into a generic label, incapable of indicating which door of the system was actually triggered, which legal interest was affected, what minimum evidence is required and what legal response is adequate. The work of this subsection is precisely to escape these two deformations. Structural exploitation needs to be preserved as a legally intelligible unit, but this unit only gains real usefulness when brought back to the dogmatic paths already available in the consumer-law microsystem.

The first axis of framing falls on the quality defect, whenever the program of functioning of the service produces a relevant loss of adequacy, continuity or functional equivalence of enjoyment. In IOCs, the question is not solved by asking whether the object <1>p. 675</1> is still formally accessible, whether the item continues to be listed in the account or whether the performance remains nominally in force. The criterion is functional. What matters is whether the service, as governed, remains capable of meeting the ends legitimately expected by the consumer or has come to frustrate them through a relevant downgrading of utility, performance, ecosystemic role or integrity of the experience. The CDC already offers this door without the need for a parallel category, because the quality defect derives precisely from the absence of properties or characteristics that allow the performance to achieve the reasonably expected ends, including when the nonconformity results from the violation of accessory duties capable of impairing, even partially, the utility of the service <2>Miragem</2><3>(Miragem, 2020, p. 523-524)</3>. The same logic is reinforced in the classical doctrine of the Code, which treats unfitness, reduction of value and inadequacy to legitimate expectation as material forms of quality defect, including when frustration manifests itself through a shorter useful life, downgraded performance or impaired utility <4>Bessa</4><5>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 348; p. 369)</5><6><7>764</7></6>.

This framing by quality defect requires a minimally objective evidentiary standard. A diffuse impression that the experience “got worse” is not enough. It is necessary to reconstruct the before and after through version records, documentation of the offer, interface evidence, history of relevant alterations and demonstration of impact on the core of enjoyment. It is at this point that functional value equivalence operates as a transversal yardstick. When the object remains only in appearance, but ceases to perform, at a substantially equivalent level, the function that justified the consumer's acquisition and remaining, the inadequacy can already be legally recognized. The system, here, does not protect the nominal survival of the performance. It protects its material capacity to satisfy the useful interest legitimately incorporated into the relationship.

There are, however, cases in which abusive teleology goes beyond functional inadequacy and approaches the safety defect of the service. This occurs when the governance program not only downgrades enjoyment, but produces relevant risk or actual harm to legal interests of a personal dimension, especially when the combination of opaque sanctions, severe reputational exclusions, erasure of history, permanent threat of loss and practical impossibility of <1>p. 676</1> challenge affects personal integrity, biographical continuity or symbolic identity. The distinction is important because the CDC already separates, in its architecture, the protection of safety and the protection of adequacy. If the core of the problem lies in downgraded enjoyment, the main lens will be that of the quality defect. If it lies in the production of intolerable risk or harm in a personal dimension, the case shifts to the logic of the safety defect. The very structure of the system prevents treating all forms of abusive governance as if they were homogeneous phenomena, and this differentiation is one of the advantages of its technical use <2>Miragem</2><3>(Miragem, 2020, p. 134-135; p. 521; p. 273)</3><4><5>765</5></4>.

The second axis of framing falls on abusive practices, and it is there that abusive teleology appears most forcefully as a repeated method of exploitation. When artificial scarcity, manufactured urgency, cycles of promise, manufacture of risk, asymmetric frictions and hindered reversibility operate predictably and repeatedly to exploit semiotic vulnerability and govern the consumer's choice, the problem no longer lies only in the final quality of the performance, but in the very way the supplier organizes the relationship. The CDC does not require literal falsity to react to this kind of mechanism. It is enough that the conduct, seen in its pattern of functioning, produces irregular conditions of negotiation and relevantly affects good faith, loyalty and balance, even if the service remains formally available and the exploitation presents itself with a varnish of technical neutrality <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 469; p. 627; p. 612)</2><3><4>766</4></3>. The point of attribution, then, is the pattern, not the isolated event.

Therefore, proof of the abusive practice cannot become a prisoner of the micro-event. It requires a combination of evidence of flow, documentation of campaigns, ecosystem rules, screenshots or recordings of the decision path, as well as demonstration that the essential was systematically obscured or subordinated to architectural pressure. The case does not need to show that a single consumer was “psychologically defeated” by the system. It needs <1>p. 677</1> to show that the environment was designed to compress deliberation, hinder exit, increase tolerance to loss and induce permanence in a context of structural asymmetry. When this pattern proves stable and replicable, the abusive practice ceases to be an impressionistic adjective and becomes an effective dogmatic door of the CDC.

The third axis is that of abusive clauses, whenever the exploitative program gains contractual institutionalization in predisposed terms, policies and acceptances. Here abusive teleology manifests itself not only in the flow or in the interface, but in the very private normative engineering that the supplier builds to reserve to itself broad powers of alteration, exclusion, discontinuation, reconfiguration and sanction without sufficient auditability, without real reciprocity and without intelligible challenge mechanisms. Contractual abusiveness, under the CDC regime, is not reduced to extravagant or openly caricatural clauses. It is also recognized when the drafting party structurally improves its contractual position, transfers risks, unilaterally broadens its power of control and breaks the minimum reciprocity that must sustain the consumer relationship <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 1045)</2><3><4>767</4></3>. If terms and policies serve as a basis for arbitrary mutations or for strategic opacities intended to preserve the supplier's superiority, they cease to be a simple contractual frame and come to function as the legal institutionalization of the exploitative program.

This control becomes even more evident when the contract reserves to the supplier excessive unilateral prerogatives to define, alter, readjust, cancel or reinterpret the very reality of enjoyment. The unilateral conception of the adhesion relationship favors, by its very structure, clauses that break material balance and weaken the consumer's contractual position. The CDC responds to this not with contractual sentimentalism, but with objective nullity of excessive unilateral advantages, of the lack of minimum transparency and of the arbitrariness of one party over the other <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 161; p. 1319-1320; p. 1242)</2><3><4>768</4></3>. The <5>p. 678</5> same perception appears in the classical reading of the system, which identifies abusive clauses as mechanisms of undue broadening of the supplier's power, assessable by the objective harm suffered by the consumer and by the material imbalance produced by the predisposed provision <6>Bessa</6><7>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, p. 581; p. 613; p. 643)</7><8><9>769</9></8>. When the exploitative program gains a contractual badge, the CDC does not retreat. It only changes the entrance door.

These three doors do not function as watertight compartments. The same case may simultaneously reveal a quality defect, an abusive practice and an abusive clause, and in borderline cases may further approach the logic of the safety defect. The decision matrix, therefore, does not serve to artificially parcel out the problem, but to guide its treatment without losing sight of the functional unity of the program. In each case, it matters to identify which mechanism predominates, which legal interest was affected, which door of the system offers the main fit, what minimum evidence is required and which remedy is most adequate. What cannot be done is to let the plurality of manifestations destroy the intelligibility of structural exploitation. When the pattern is repeated, legal classification needs to preserve the program as a relevant unit, and not pretend that everything comes down to small disconnected deviations.
